strengths: The paper identifies a real and important evaluation hazard in brain-to-text decoding: repeated text stimuli across train/test can let strong autoregressive decoders memorize targets rather than use neural signals.
The distinction between brain-signal leakage and text-stimulus leakage is useful, and the graph-based framing helps make split constraints explicit for EEG and fMRI datasets.

The empirical stress tests are relevant: additional leakage-free test sets, shuffled brain inputs, and longer-training experiments all support the claim that prior scores can be substantially inflated.
Re-evaluating UniCoRN and EEG2Text on Narratives and ZuCo provides a potentially useful starting benchmark for future work.
weaknesses: The paper overstates its central claim. Calling all prior cross-subject splits "wrong" assumes that the only valid task is generalization to both unseen subjects and unseen stimuli; same-stimulus/new-subject decoding is a different evaluation target, not automatically invalid.

Several formal definitions and metrics appear imprecise or erroneous, including leakage definitions using universal quantification where existential leakage is intended, and BSLR/TSLR formulas whose set intersections and normalizations are hard to interpret.

The proposed split discards data and changes subject/story/text distributions, but the paper does not report retained sample counts, split sizes, or distributional shifts, making comparisons partly confounded.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the construction of the additional test set, exact preprocessing, split indices, code availability, and model-selection details are insufficiently specified; most model results lack multi-seed variance or significance testing.

The evidence for brain-signal leakage harming the encoder is weak. Validation loss is only an indirect proxy, the EEG results are inconclusive, and no independent representation or cross-subject generalization metric is provided.

The proposed method is presented as the correct criterion rather than one stringent benchmark protocol, and the paper gives little guidance on when less restrictive protocols may still answer legitimate scientific questions.
The contribution is useful and likely fixable, but current rigor and framing concerns prevent a clear Findings recommendation.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and practically consequential evaluation problem in cross-subject brain-to-text decoding: subject overlap and stimulus/text overlap can make reported decoding results largely reflect memorization rather than neural decoding.

The central criterion is intuitive and relevant: a cross-subject benchmark should prevent both test-subject brain signals and test text stimuli from appearing in training data. The graph formalization helps expose how common split strategies create leakage.

The empirical case is fairly broad for this niche: experiments cover fMRI and EEG datasets, two representative SOTA models, leakage-rate measurements, an additional leakage-free test set, shuffled-input controls, teacher-forcing checks, and longer-training analyses.

The results consistently show large drops under leakage-free evaluation and near-preserved performance with shuffled inputs under leaky splits, which strongly supports the claim that prior split choices can overestimate performance.
The paper is timely and relevant to NLP evaluation, especially for neuro-symbolic or brain-to-language generation work where benchmark construction is central to scientific validity.
weaknesses: The strongest claims are overgeneralized. The paper says all current splitting methods are wrong, but it mainly analyzes a small set of split categories, two datasets, and two models; some supposedly leaky setups may correspond to different valid tasks, such as within-subject or seen-stimulus evaluation, rather than being intrinsically invalid.

The proposed split is insufficiently characterized as a benchmark. The paper does not clearly report retained versus discarded sample counts, subject/story/text distributions, or whether the discarded data changes dataset difficulty or introduces selection bias.

Reproducibility is only partial. The manuscript gives hyperparameters and pseudocode, but does not appear to provide exact split files, code, data indices, or full random-seed details for the main model results; main performance tables also lack standard deviations or statistical tests.

The formal leakage definitions are not fully precise. For example, the definitions use very strong universal quantification where an existential train-test overlap would normally define leakage, and the pseudocode in the appendix is difficult to follow and appears underspecified in places.

The evidence for encoder-side damage is weaker than the evidence for decoder memorization. Validation loss is an indirect proxy for representation quality, and the EEG results do not support the same conclusion about brain-signal leakage.

Evaluation remains limited to automatic n-gram metrics and a small set of existing models. More semantic evaluation, qualitative output analysis, and stronger baselines would make the benchmark claims more convincing.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and plausible evaluation flaw in cross-subject brain-to-text decoding: subject leakage and stimulus-text leakage can make reported generation scores largely reflect memorization rather than decoding from neural signals.
The graph-based framing cleanly formalizes why common split strategies fail and gives an intuitive criterion for leakage-free cross-subject evaluation across EEG and fMRI settings.

The empirical evidence is fairly compelling for the decoder-side claim: additional leakage-free test sets and shuffled-input experiments show large BLEU/ROUGE drops under leaky splits, while the proposed split behaves more consistently.
The work re-evaluates representative prior systems, EEG2Text and UniCoRN, on public datasets, making the paper relevant as a corrective benchmark for a small but important NLP/neuroscience subarea.

The appendices include useful extra checks, including teacher-forcing and longer-training analyses, which strengthen the claim that the observed effects are not only an artifact of one decoding setup.
weaknesses: The central claim that all current cross-subject splitting methods are wrong is overstated. The paper examines a limited set of split categories, two models, and two datasets, and does not fully distinguish invalid evaluation from alternative task definitions where test subjects share stimuli by design.

Reproducibility is incomplete for a benchmark-style paper: there is no visible code or split-file release, exact retained/discarded sample counts are not reported, and construction details for the additional test set are under-specified.

The proposed method discards data, but the paper does not quantify how much data is lost per dataset/split or analyze whether distribution shift and reduced training size contribute to the lower scores under the leakage-free benchmark.

The encoder-side evidence is weaker than the decoder-side evidence. Validation loss is only an indirect proxy for representation quality, and the EEG results do not clearly support the stated brain-signal leakage story.

The experimental reporting lacks uncertainty estimates or significance tests for the main decoding results, despite stochastic splitting and training. This limits confidence in smaller differences, especially in the fair benchmark table.
Some formal definitions and pseudocode are hard to follow and appear imprecise in places, which matters because the main contribution is a data-splitting criterion and algorithm.

The evaluation relies almost entirely on BLEU and ROUGE, which are limited for brain-to-text semantic reconstruction; more semantic metrics or qualitative analyses would better support the practical conclusions.

The benchmark would be stronger with simple decoder-only, retrieval, language-model, and random-baseline controls, plus qualitative examples showing memorized versus genuinely decoded outputs.

The proposed split criterion, at the conceptual level, is simple and useful: evaluation should hold out both subjects and stimuli when the stated goal is generalization to unseen neural responses and unseen text.
weaknesses: I would not recommend this for main-conference publication in its current form, and it is only borderline for Findings because reproducibility and formal precision are not yet adequate.

The paper overclaims. Calling all current cross-subject splits wrong conflates different evaluation goals: holding out subjects while keeping stimuli fixed can be a legitimate subject-generalization benchmark if presented as such. The paper should distinguish subject generalization, stimulus generalization, and joint subject-stimulus generalization.

Several formal definitions and equations appear incorrect or at least badly specified. For example, the leakage definitions use universal quantification where existential conditions seem intended, and the BSLR/TSLR formulas refer to intersections of train/test sets in ways that would be empty for disjoint sample sets unless additional matching semantics are assumed.

The proposed algorithms are not reproducible as written. The appendix pseudocode has indexing/dimensional inconsistencies, unclear loop semantics, and an admitted variable-name simplification that makes implementation ambiguous.

The empirical analysis relies almost entirely on BLEU/ROUGE. These are useful for detecting memorization but insufficient for evaluating semantic reconstruction quality in brain-to-text decoding; stronger semantic metrics or qualitative analyses would improve the benchmark claim.

The encoder-side evidence is weaker than the decoder-side evidence. Validation loss is an indirect proxy for representation quality, and the EEG results do not clearly support the proposed brain-signal-leakage interpretation.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and practically consequential evaluation problem in cross-subject brain-to-text decoding: subject overlap and, especially, repeated text stimuli can make reported decoding scores largely reflect memorization rather than neural decoding.

The central claim is supported from several angles: formal analysis of common splitting strategies, leakage-rate measurements on Narratives and ZuCo, additional held-out test sets, shuffled-input controls, and longer-training experiments. The shuffled-input results are particularly persuasive evidence that leaked text stimuli can dominate the decoder.

The proposed splitting criterion is conceptually simple and well aligned with the intended generalization setting: held-out subjects and held-out stimuli should both be absent from training. Re-evaluating UniCoRN and EEG2Text under this criterion provides a useful corrective benchmark for future work.

The paper is relevant to NLP and computational cognitive modeling, and its contribution is valuable even without a new architecture because it challenges the validity of prior evaluation protocols in a growing brain-to-language literature.
weaknesses: The claim that all current cross-subject splitting methods are wrong is somewhat overbroad. The paper analyzes a useful taxonomy and two representative models/datasets, but it does not exhaustively verify all prior protocols or possible leakage-free variants used in the literature.

Some formal definitions and algorithms are not fully rigorous. The leakage definitions appear to use universal quantification where existential overlap would be the natural condition, and the pseudocode contains confusing indexing and split constraints, especially for the fMRI case. This weakens confidence that independent readers could implement the exact intended procedure from the paper alone.

Reproducibility is only moderate. The manuscript gives hyperparameters and pseudocode, but does not provide code, exact split indices, retained/discarded sample counts, or the construction details for the additional test sets. These are crucial for a paper whose contribution is an evaluation protocol and benchmark.

The empirical evaluation is convincing but narrow: only two datasets and two main model families are tested, decoding metrics are limited to BLEU/ROUGE, and most downstream decoding scores lack variance or statistical testing across split seeds.

The encoder-side analysis is less convincing than the decoder-side analysis. Interpreting continuously decreasing validation loss as evidence of degraded representation ability is not well justified; it shows possible leakage-induced memorization, but the causal story about encoder quality remains underdeveloped.

Presentation is generally understandable, but the writing sometimes uses imprecise language such as “right/wrong” splitting and contains grammatical issues. The paper would be stronger with more precise terminology and clearer separation between proven leakage conditions, empirical observations, and broader recommendations.

Requiring both unseen subjects and unseen text may be appropriate for open-ended brain-to-text decoding, but the paper does not justify why this should be the sole valid cross-subject benchmark, nor does it discuss what scientific questions same-stimulus cross-subject splits can validly answer.

The paper is relevant to NLP/CL because it directly concerns evaluation validity for language generation from neural signals, and the re-evaluation of EEG2Text and UniCoRN would be useful if made reproducible.
The distinction between subject leakage and stimulus leakage is helpful, and the graph-based framing makes the dataset-splitting issue easier to reason about.
weaknesses: The central claim is overstated. The manuscript repeatedly says existing splitting methods are simply wrong and evaluations are meaningless, but some prior settings may validly test generalization to new subjects under seen stimuli. The proposed split instead tests joint generalization to new subjects and new text, which is a stricter but different task.

The formal definitions contain apparent quantifier and set-membership errors. Brain/text leakage are defined with universal conditions where existential overlap would be appropriate, and the BSLR/TSLR formulas appear to use intersections of disjoint train/test sample sets rather than subject- or stimulus-level overlap. This weakens the claimed theoretical rigor.

The proposed splitting algorithms are underspecified and somewhat inconsistent. The pseudocode has indexing/dimension issues, relies on assumptions such as M>N or K<N, and does not report how much data is discarded, whether final split ratios remain close to 80/10/10, or how balanced the resulting subject/story/text distributions are.

The experiments show that leakage inflates metrics, but they do not fully disentangle failure modes: lower scores under the proposed split could reflect harder unseen-text generation, fewer training examples, distribution shift from discarded data, subject transfer difficulty, or model weakness.
